sections.title: The Gateway: Why do humans everywhere invent games with rules that don't matter, and then care about them so much?
sections.html:
Web address: /sports/why-we-play/ · Keywords: sports and games, why we play, history of sport, types of sports, Indian games

Nobody needs to put a ball through a hoop. Nobody needs to checkmate a king made of wood. Yet billions of people play, watch and argue about games every day. India stops for a cricket final; Brazil stops for football; a whole hall falls silent for a chess move.

This short course asks one question in seven steps: why do humans play, and why do games matter so much to us? It goes from the oldest board game in the world to the Olympics, from chess's journey out of India to esports, and from the science of fandom to the question of what counts as a sport. Each page takes about two minutes.

By the end you will be able to:

  • Say what makes something a game, and what makes a game a sport.
  • Tell the story of chess from India to the world.
  • Explain why the ancient Olympics stopped and how they came back.
  • Describe why fans feel a win in their own body.
  • Take a side, with reasons, on whether video games are a sport.

sections.title: What was the first game?
sections.html:
Short answer: Running, wrestling and chasing games are surely older than history, because even young animals play-fight. The oldest game we can still play from its own board is the Royal Game of Ur, from Mesopotamia, about 4,600 years old; the Egyptian game senet is older still.

Keywords: first game ever, oldest board game, Royal Game of Ur, senet, history of games

Play is older than humans

Puppies wrestle, crows slide down snowy roofs, and young chimpanzees play chase. Biologists think play trains bodies and brains for real life while keeping everyone safe. So human games began long before anyone wrote them down: races, wrestling, throwing at targets, hide-and-seek.

The oldest boards

  • Senet (Egypt): boards appear in tombs from about 3100 BCE; Tutankhamun was buried with several.
  • The Royal Game of Ur (Mesopotamia): beautiful boards found by Leonard Woolley in the Royal Cemetery of Ur, about 2600 BCE. In the 1980s the British Museum curator Irving Finkel worked out its rules from a cuneiform tablet written in 177 BCE.
  • Mancala (Africa and Asia): "count-and-capture" games played with seeds in pits; India's pallanguzhi is one.

Games in ancient India

Dice made of bone and the vibhitaka nut appear in the Rig Veda's "Gambler's Hymn". The Mahabharata turns on a game of dice. Game boards were scratched into the steps of temples and forts.

Remember this: Play is older than humans; the oldest games we can still play were invented in the first cities.

sections.title: Why does every culture have a ball game?
sections.html:
Short answer: A ball is the simplest object that moves in surprising ways: it rolls, bounces and flies. That makes it perfect for skill, teamwork and chance, so peoples who never met each other invented ball games again and again.

Keywords: history of ball games, Mesoamerican ballgame, cuju, origin of football, why ball games are popular

Many ball games, many places

  • Mesoamerica: rubber balls from about 1650 BCE; the ballgame (ōllamaliztli) was played on stone courts and sometimes linked to ritual sacrifice. Rubber, unknown in Europe then, made balls that bounced high.
  • China: cuju ("kick ball"), played from the Han dynasty; FIFA recognises it as the earliest documented form of football.
  • Japan: kemari, a courtly game of keeping a ball in the air.
  • India: gend-balla and many village ball games; Manipur's sagol kangjei (polo on horseback) and yubi lakpi (rugby with a greased coconut).
  • North America: the Haudenosaunee game that the French called lacrosse.

Why a ball works

A ball turns physics into drama. It can be passed, so it creates teamwork; it can be stolen, so it creates contest; it can bounce wrongly, so it creates luck. And it is cheap: a bundle of rags, a coconut or a pig's bladder will do.

From folk games to world sports

In 19th-century Britain, schools and clubs wrote down rules: football (1863), rugby (1871), lawn tennis (1870s). Railways, newspapers and the British Empire then carried these rules around the world.

Remember this: The ball is the world's favourite toy because it mixes skill, teamwork and luck.

Next: Some games travelled even further than the ball. The greatest traveller began in India.

sections.title: How did chess travel from India to the world?
sections.html:
Short answer: Chess began in India as chaturanga around the 6th century CE, during or just after the Gupta period. It went to Persia as shatranj, spread with the Arab world to Europe, and took its modern rules in Spain around 1475, when the queen became the strongest piece.

Keywords: origin of chess, chaturanga, shatranj, history of chess, chess in India

Chaturanga: a model army

Chaturanga means "four limbs", the four divisions of an Indian army: infantry, cavalry, elephants and chariots. These became the pawn, knight, bishop and rook. Its king was the raja, with a counsellor beside him.

Persia and the Arab world

By the 7th century the game was played in Sassanid Persia as chatrang, later shatranj. The Persian Shahnameh tells how an Indian king sent it as a riddle to the Persian court. Words came with it: "check" from the Persian shah (king), "checkmate" from shah mat (the king is helpless).

Europe and the modern queen

Shatranj entered Europe through Muslim Spain and Sicily around 1000 CE. Around 1475, Spanish and Italian players made the queen and the bishop long-range pieces; the faster game was called "the queen's chess".

Back home

Chess also travelled east to become Chinese xiangqi, Japanese shogi and Thai makruk. In 2024 India won both gold medals at the Chess Olympiad and D. Gukesh became the youngest undisputed world champion at 18. The game came home.

Remember this: Chaturanga's army of four parts became the world's most played thinking game.

Next: Chess spread for 1,500 years. The Olympics, by contrast, vanished for 1,500 years. Why?

sections.title: Why did the Olympics stop for 1,500 years?
sections.html:
Short answer: The ancient Olympic Games at Olympia (by tradition from 776 BCE) were a religious festival for Zeus. When the Roman Empire became Christian, pagan festivals were banned, and the Games ended around 393 CE. Pierre de Coubertin revived them in Athens in 1896.

Keywords: ancient Olympics, why Olympics ended, Pierre de Coubertin, first modern Olympics 1896

The ancient Games

Every four years Greek city-states held a truce so athletes could travel safely to Olympia. Events included running, wrestling, boxing, the pentathlon, chariot racing and the brutal pankration. Winners got an olive wreath, and fame. Married women were not allowed to watch.

The end

Emperor Theodosius I banned pagan cults in the 390s; the traditional date for the last ancient Games is 393 CE, though some scholars think they lingered into the 5th century. Earthquakes and floods later buried the site.

The revival

The Frenchman Pierre de Coubertin believed sport could build character and peace between nations. He founded the International Olympic Committee in 1894; the first modern Games were held in Athens in 1896, with 241 athletes, all men. Women competed from 1900 (Paris); the British tennis player Charlotte Cooper was the first woman Olympic champion.

India and the Olympics

Norman Pritchard won two silver medals in athletics for India in 1900. India sent its first official team in 1920 and won its first hockey gold in 1928.

Remember this: The Olympics were sacred, then forbidden, then reborn as a world festival.

sections.title: What makes a sport a sport?
sections.html:
Short answer: Most definitions agree that a sport is a game of skill, with physical effort, rules and fair competition, organised by a governing body. The edges are fuzzy: chess, darts and esports call themselves sports too, and the IOC recognises chess and bridge as "sports of the mind".

Keywords: definition of sport, what is a sport, is chess a sport, game vs sport

Game, play and sport

  • Play is free activity done for its own sake.
  • A game adds rules and a goal. The philosopher Bernard Suits defined it as "the voluntary attempt to overcome unnecessary obstacles": golf would be easier if you could carry the ball to the hole.
  • A sport is a game where skill is tested, usually with the body, in organised competition.

The tests people use

  1. Is there physical skill or effort?
  2. Are there fixed rules and a fair way to decide the winner?
  3. Is there a governing body and regular competition?
  4. Does skill matter more than luck?

Football passes every test. Snakes and Ladders fails test 4. Chess fails test 1 for some people and passes it for others, because elite chess is physically exhausting. The IOC has recognised chess (FIDE, since 1999) and bridge (the World Bridge Federation) as sports.

Why it matters

Recognition brings money, school places, Olympic dreams and government support. That is why yoga, kabaddi, kho-kho, esports and mallakhamb have all argued to be counted.

Remember this: A sport is skill plus rules plus fair competition; the borders are argued, not fixed.

sections.title: Why do fans feel a win in their own body?
sections.html:
Short answer: Fans identify with their team, so the brain treats its wins and losses partly as their own. Heart rate and stress hormones rise during big matches, and a win can feel like personal success. Psychologists call it "basking in reflected glory".

Keywords: sports fan psychology, why fans care, basking in reflected glory, fandom science

"We won", "they lost"

In a famous study (Robert Cialdini and colleagues, 1976), American students wore more university clothing after their football team won, and said "we won", but "they lost" after a defeat. This is BIRGing (Basking In Reflected Glory) and its opposite, CORFing (Cutting Off Reflected Failure).

The body joins in

Studies of football fans have found raised heart rates and stress hormones during penalty shoot-outs; hospital visits for heart trouble rose in Germany on the days of tense 2006 World Cup matches (Wilbert-Lampen and colleagues, 2008). Fans' brains respond to their team's success in reward areas.

Belonging

Fandom gives people a tribe, a calendar of rituals and shared memories across generations. A grandfather and grandchild may have little in common, except the 1983 or 2011 World Cup.

The dark side

The same feelings can turn into hatred of rivals, violence and online abuse of players. Healthy fandom keeps the joy and lets go of the hate.

Remember this: Fans borrow the team's glory and pain, because belonging is part of being human.

sections.title: Are video games a sport?
sections.html:
Short answer: Competitive video gaming, called esports, has leagues, teams, coaches, prize money and fans in the hundreds of millions, and it was a medal event at the 2022 Asian Games. Whether it is a "sport" depends on the definition; it is certainly a skill competition.

Keywords: are esports a sport, esports Asian Games, gaming as a career, esports in India

What esports is

Professional players compete in games such as League of Legends, Dota 2, Counter-Strike, Valorant, FIFA/EA Sports FC and, in India, BGMI and Free Fire. The finals fill stadiums. The first known video-game tournament was held at Stanford University in 1972 (Spacewar!).

For

Elite players need fast reactions, hand-eye skill, teamwork, strategy and training of eight hours or more a day. Esports were a demonstration event at the 2018 Asian Games and medal events in 2022 (Hangzhou). The IOC has announced plans for Olympic esports events.

Against

The physical effort is small compared with running or wrestling; the games are owned by companies, which can change or end them; and there are worries about screen time, addiction and gambling.

In India

India's Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025 bans real-money online games while promoting esports and social games. Esports is a growing career, but a narrow one: only a few make a living.

Remember this: Esports is skill competition at a high level; whether it is "sport" is a definition fight.

sections.title: Recap: the story of sports and games in one page
sections.html:
Short answer: Humans play because play trains us, bonds us and delights us. Games began with races and wrestling, grew into board games in the first cities, ball games on every continent, codified sports in 19th-century Britain, the modern Olympics in 1896, and digital games today.

Keywords: history of sports summary, sports explained, types of games

  1. Play is older than humans.
  2. First boards: senet and the Royal Game of Ur (about 3000–2600 BCE).
  3. Ancient festivals: Olympia (776 BCE), Mesoamerican ballgames, Indian dice and chaturanga.
  4. Codification (19th century): football, rugby, tennis, badminton and many others get written rules and governing bodies.
  5. Modern Olympics (1896), then world championships, leagues, TV and money.
  6. Women's sport and parasports grow through the 20th and 21st centuries.
  7. Digital games and esports (from 1972).

Remember this: Games have rules that don't "matter", which is exactly why they can teach us what does.

sections.title: Team ball games
sections.html:
Before you start — SPT-02. Many team ball games share one family tree: the folk football of medieval Europe split in 19th-century England into association football (soccer) and rugby, which in turn gave rise to American, Canadian and Australian codes. Hockey and its cousins are stick-and-ball games.

  • Association football (soccer): two teams of 11; rules set by the Football Association, London, 1863; governed by FIFA (founded Paris, 1904) and the IFAB (law-makers, 1886); the world's most popular sport. Olympic.
  • Futsal and beach soccer: five-a-side indoor football (FIFA) and sand football.
  • Rugby union: 15 players; the "William Webb Ellis ran with the ball at Rugby School, 1823" story is a legend; Rugby Football Union 1871; World Rugby. Rugby sevens is Olympic (since 2016).
  • Rugby league: 13 players; split from union in 1895 in northern England over payments to players.
  • American football: from rugby and soccer at US colleges (1869 onward); Walter Camp's rules; the NFL (1920) and the Super Bowl (1967).
  • Canadian football, Australian rules football (Melbourne, 1859; the AFL), Gaelic football (Ireland; the GAA, 1884).

  • Field hockey: 11 a side, stick and hard ball; modern rules in England (1886); FIH (1924); India won eight Olympic golds (1928–1956, 1964, 1980) and bronze in 2020 and 2024. Olympic.
  • Ice hockey: see SPT-07. Bandy: hockey on ice with a ball (Russia, Sweden).
  • Hurling and camogie (Ireland, ancient): fast game with a hurley and sliotar.
  • Lacrosse: from the Haudenosaunee and other First Nations; returns to the Olympics at Los Angeles 2028 (sixes).
  • Polo: modern polo was learned by British officers from Manipur (sagol kangjei) in the 1850s–60s; the Calcutta Polo Club (1862) is among the oldest in the world. See SPT-09.
  • Shinty (Scotland) and golf (see SPT-09).

  • Beach volleyball (Olympic since 1996), Gaelic handball, ultimate frisbee (flying disc, self-refereed "spirit of the game"), flag football (non-contact American football, Olympic from 2028), tchoukball.
  • Kabaddi and kho-kho: Indian team chase games played outdoors and indoors; see SPT-17.

sections.title: Bat-and-ball games
sections.html:
Before you start — SPT-03. Bat-and-ball games share a pattern: one side bats and scores runs, the other bowls or pitches and fields. Cricket, baseball and rounders may have common roots in English folk games such as stoolball.
  • SPT-03.1 Cricket: 11 a side; England, 16th century; the Laws are kept by the MCC (from 1788); governed by the ICC (founded 1909 as the Imperial Cricket Conference; HQ Dubai). Formats: Test (first Test, Melbourne, 1877), One-Day International (1971; first World Cup 1975, won by West Indies), Twenty20 (2003; first T20 World Cup 2007, won by India). Returns to the Olympics at Los Angeles 2028 (T20). India's men won the T20 World Cup in 2007, 2024 and 2026 (final against New Zealand, 8 March 2026), the ODI World Cup in 1983 and 2011, and the Champions Trophy in 2002 (shared), 2013 and 2025; India's women won their first ODI World Cup in 2025.
  • SPT-03.2 Leagues: the Indian Premier League (2008; Royal Challengers Bengaluru won in 2025 and 2026), Big Bash (Australia), The Hundred (England), Women's Premier League (India, 2023), Pakistan Super League, Caribbean Premier League.
  • SPT-03.3 Baseball: 9 a side; from English bat-and-ball games, shaped in New York (the Knickerbocker rules, 1845); Major League Baseball (1903 World Series); hugely popular in the USA, Japan, Korea, Cuba, the Dominican Republic; World Baseball Classic (2006). Olympic at some Games (returns 2028).
  • SPT-03.4 Softball: larger ball, underarm pitching; Olympic at some Games.
  • SPT-03.5 Rounders (Britain, Ireland), stoolball (England), pesäpallo (Finnish baseball), lapta (Russia).
  • SPT-03.6 Gilli-danda and street cricket: India's stick-and-peg game and the gully cricket of lanes and rooftops (see SPT-17).

sections.title: Racket sports on open courts
sections.html:
Before you start — SPT-04. Racket sports grew from the medieval French jeu de paume ("game of the palm") and real tennis. Lawn tennis was patented in 1874. Badminton, table tennis and squash are mostly indoor and appear in SPT-10.
  • SPT-04.1 Tennis: singles or doubles on grass, clay or hard courts; Major Walter Clopton Wingfield's sphairistike (1873–74); the first Wimbledon (1877, won by Spencer Gore); the four Grand Slams (Australian Open, Roland-Garros, Wimbledon, US Open); ITF (1913), ATP and WTA tours; Davis Cup (1900), Billie Jean King Cup. Olympic. Indian stars: Ramanathan Krishnan, Vijay Amritraj, Leander Paes (Olympic bronze 1996), Mahesh Bhupathi, Sania Mirza, Rohan Bopanna.
  • SPT-04.2 Real tennis (court tennis): the indoor ancestor, still played in a few historic courts.
  • SPT-04.3 Padel: doubles in a walled court (Mexico, 1969); fast-growing in Spain, Argentina and the Gulf.
  • SPT-04.4 Pickleball: paddle game invented on Bainbridge Island, Washington (1965); the fastest-growing sport in the USA in the 2020s.
  • SPT-04.5 Beach tennis, platform tennis, soft tennis (Japan, Korea).

sections.title: Athletics (track and field, road and cross-country)
sections.html:
Before you start — SPT-05. "Athletics" is the oldest sport family: run, jump, throw. World Athletics (founded 1912 as the IAAF) governs it. It is the heart of the Olympic programme.
  • SPT-05.1 Sprints and hurdles: 100 m to 400 m; Usain Bolt's 100 m world record of 9.58 s (Berlin, 2009); Florence Griffith-Joyner's 10.49 s (1988).
  • SPT-05.2 Middle and long distance: 800 m to 10,000 m, steeplechase; the "four-minute mile" broken by Roger Bannister (1954).
  • SPT-05.3 Marathon and road running: from the legend of Pheidippides; the distance was fixed at 42.195 km in 1921 (from the 1908 London Olympics course); Eliud Kipchoge's sub-two-hour run (an unofficial event, Vienna 2019); Mumbai Marathon (2004).
  • SPT-05.4 Relays: 4 × 100 m, 4 × 400 m, mixed relays.
  • SPT-05.5 Jumps: high jump (the Fosbury Flop, 1968), pole vault (Armand Duplantis's repeated world records), long jump, triple jump.
  • SPT-05.6 Throws: shot put, discus, hammer, javelin. Neeraj Chopra won India's first Olympic gold in athletics (javelin, Tokyo 2020), silver at Paris 2024 and the 2023 world title.
  • SPT-05.7 Combined events: decathlon (men), heptathlon (women).
  • SPT-05.8 Race walking, cross-country, trail and ultra running, mountain running.
  • SPT-05.9 Indian athletics legends: Milkha Singh ("The Flying Sikh"), P. T. Usha (fourth in the 400 m hurdles, 1984, by 1/100 of a second), Anju Bobby George (world championship bronze, 2003), Hima Das, Avinash Sable.

sections.title: Water sports
sections.html:
Before you start — SPT-06. Water sports include racing in, on and under water. World Aquatics (founded 1908 as FINA) governs swimming, diving, water polo, artistic and open-water swimming.
  • SPT-06.1 Swimming: freestyle, backstroke, breaststroke, butterfly, medley; Michael Phelps won 23 Olympic golds; Katie Ledecky; Indian swimmers Mihir Sen (Palk Strait, 1966), Sajan Prakash, Srihari Nataraj.
  • SPT-06.2 Diving, artistic swimming, water polo, open-water marathon swimming.
  • SPT-06.3 Rowing: the Oxford–Cambridge Boat Race (1829); World Rowing; Olympic.
  • SPT-06.4 Canoe and kayak: sprint and slalom; dragon boat racing (China).
  • SPT-06.5 Sailing: dinghies, keelboats, windsurfing and kitefoiling; the America's Cup (1851), the oldest international trophy in sport.
  • SPT-06.6 Surfing: from ancient Hawaii (heʻe nalu); Duke Kahanamoku; Olympic from 2020; India's surfing coast at Mulki (Karnataka) and Kovalam.
  • SPT-06.7 Traditional boat races: Kerala's vallam kali snake-boat races (the Nehru Trophy on Punnamada Lake since 1952); Indonesia's pacu jalur.
  • SPT-06.8 Other water sports: water skiing, wakeboarding, jet ski, underwater hockey, free diving, fishing (sport angling).

sections.title: Winter sports
sections.html:
Before you start — SPT-07. Snow and ice sports grew in Scandinavia, the Alps and North America. The first Winter Olympics were at Chamonix (1924). At Milano Cortina 2026 (6–22 February 2026) Norway topped the medal table.
  • SPT-07.1 Skiing: alpine (downhill, slalom), Nordic (cross-country), ski jumping, freestyle, biathlon (skiing plus shooting); governed by FIS.
  • SPT-07.2 Snowboarding: from the 1960s–70s "snurfer"; Olympic since 1998.
  • SPT-07.3 Skating: figure skating, speed skating, short track; ISU (1892).
  • SPT-07.4 Ice hockey: Montreal, 1875 (first organised indoor game); NHL (1917); Canada, USA, Russia, Sweden, Finland, Czechia.
  • SPT-07.5 Sliding sports: bobsleigh, luge, skeleton; India's Shiva Keshavan competed in luge at six Winter Olympics.
  • SPT-07.6 Curling: Scotland, 16th century; "chess on ice".
  • SPT-07.7 Winter sports in India: Gulmarg and Auli for skiing; the Khelo India Winter Games (since 2020) in Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh; ice hockey in Ladakh.
sections.summary: -  SPT-07.1 Skiing: alpine (downhill, slalom), Nordic (cross-country), ski jumping, freestyle, biathlon (skiing plus shooting); governed by FIS.

sections.title: Motor sports and air sports
sections.html:
Before you start — SPT-08. Motor sports race cars, bikes, boats and more; the FIA (cars, 1904) and FIM (motorcycles, 1904) govern most. Air sports are governed by the FAI (1905).
  • SPT-08.1 Formula One: the world championship began in 1950 (first race at Silverstone; first champion Giuseppe Farina); Michael Schumacher and Lewis Hamilton each won seven titles; Lando Norris won the 2025 title. India hosted the Indian Grand Prix at the Buddh International Circuit (2011–2013); Narain Karthikeyan (2005) and Karun Chandhok are India's F1 drivers.
  • SPT-08.2 Other car racing: endurance (24 Hours of Le Mans, 1923), IndyCar (Indianapolis 500, 1911), NASCAR, rallying (WRC; the Dakar Rally), touring cars, karting, Formula E (electric, 2014).
  • SPT-08.3 Motorcycle racing: MotoGP (world championship since 1949), Isle of Man TT (1907), motocross, speedway, superbike; India's Harith Noah and C. S. Santosh at the Dakar.
  • SPT-08.4 Powerboat racing and air racing.
  • SPT-08.5 Air sports: gliding, paragliding (Bir Billing, Himachal, hosted the Paragliding World Cup in 2015), hang gliding, skydiving, ballooning, aerobatics, drone racing.

sections.title: Adventure, equestrian and target sports
sections.html:
Before you start — SPT-09. Three outdoor families: adventure and extreme (pushing against nature), equestrian (horse and rider together), and target (precision).

  • Mountaineering: Everest first climbed by Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay (29 May 1953); Bachendri Pal the first Indian woman on top (1984); Arunima Sinha the first woman amputee (2013).
  • Sport climbing (Olympic since 2020), bouldering, trekking, orienteering.
  • Triathlon (1974 onward; Olympic since 2000) and the Ironman (Hawaii, 1978); duathlon, adventure racing.
  • Cycling: road (Tour de France, 1903), track, mountain bike, BMX; UCI (1900).
  • Skateboarding (Olympic since 2020), parkour, inline skating, roller sports.
  • Extreme sports: base jumping, wingsuit flying, big-wave surfing, ice climbing; the X Games (1995).

  • Olympic equestrian: dressage, show jumping, eventing; men and women compete together; FEI (1921).
  • Polo (see SPT-02.2) and horse racing (the Derby at Epsom, 1780; the Indian Derby, Mumbai; flat racing, steeplechase).
  • Endurance riding, vaulting, tent pegging (cavalry sport popular in India and Pakistan), buzkashi (Central Asia).

  • Archery: World Archery (1931); Olympic; Korea's dominance; India's Deepika Kumari; Sheetal Devi in para archery (SPT-19).
  • Shooting: rifle, pistol, shotgun; ISSF; Abhinav Bindra won India's first individual Olympic gold (10 m air rifle, Beijing 2008); Manu Bhaker won two bronzes at Paris 2024, the first Indian to win two medals at one Games after independence.
  • Golf: Scotland, 15th century; St Andrews; the R&A and USGA set rules; the four men's majors (The Masters, PGA Championship, US Open, The Open); Olympic again since 2016; Aditi Ashok fourth at Tokyo 2020.
  • Bowls (lawn bowls), pétanque, bocce, croquet, disc golf: precision games of rolling and throwing.

parts.title: Physical Sports: Indoor
parts.intro: About this Part. Sports usually played under a roof: court and racket games, gymnastics and strength, combat and martial arts, cue sports, bowling and darts. Several (volleyball, kabaddi, futsal) are played both indoors and out.

sections.title: Indoor court and racket games
sections.html:
Before you start — SPT-10. Several of these were invented on purpose by teachers or officers who needed a game for a hall or a rainy season.
  • SPT-10.1 Badminton: shuttlecock over a high net; played by British officers in Poona (Pune) in the 1870s, named after the Duke of Beaufort's Badminton House; BWF (founded 1934 as the IBF); the All England Championships (1899); Olympic since 1992. India: Prakash Padukone (All England 1980), Pullela Gopichand (All England 2001), Saina Nehwal (Olympic bronze 2012), P. V. Sindhu (Olympic silver 2016, bronze 2020; world champion 2019), Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty, Lakshya Sen.
  • SPT-10.2 Table tennis: "ping-pong" from Victorian England (1880s); ITTF (1926); Olympic since 1988; China's dominance; the "Ping-Pong Diplomacy" between the USA and China (1971); India's Sharath Kamal, Manika Batra.
  • SPT-10.3 Squash: from Harrow School, England (about 1830); World Squash, PSA tour; joins the Olympics at Los Angeles 2028; India's Saurav Ghosal, Joshna Chinappa, Dipika Pallikal.
  • SPT-10.4 Basketball: invented by James Naismith in Springfield, Massachusetts (December 1891) with peach baskets; FIBA (1932); the NBA (1946); 3×3 basketball is Olympic since 2020.
  • SPT-10.5 Volleyball: invented by William G. Morgan in Holyoke, Massachusetts (1895) as "Mintonette"; FIVB (1947); Olympic since 1964; huge in Brazil, Italy, Poland, Japan; Kerala's village volleyball culture.
  • SPT-10.6 Handball: Denmark and Germany, around 1900; IHF; Olympic; very popular in Europe.
  • SPT-10.7 Netball: from early women's basketball (1890s); strong in England, Australia, New Zealand, Jamaica; Commonwealth Games sport.
  • SPT-10.8 Futsal, floorball, korfball (Dutch mixed-gender game), sepak takraw (kick volleyball of South-East Asia; also outdoors), throwball (India), tenniquoit (ring tennis).

sections.title: Gymnastics, strength and fitness sports
sections.html:
Before you start — SPT-11. Sports of the body's control and power. Gymnastics comes from the German Turnen movement of Friedrich Ludwig Jahn (1810s); FIG (1881) is the oldest international sports federation still in existence.
  • SPT-11.1 Artistic gymnastics: floor, vault, bars, beam, rings, pommel horse; Nadia Comăneci's first perfect 10 (1976); Simone Biles; India's Dipa Karmakar (fourth in vault, Rio 2016).
  • SPT-11.2 Rhythmic gymnastics, trampoline, acrobatic and aerobic gymnastics, parkour (FIG discipline).
  • SPT-11.3 Mallakhamb: Indian pole and rope gymnastics from Maharashtra; revived by Balambhatdada Deodhar in the 19th century; now in the National Games and Khelo India; also SPT-17.
  • SPT-11.4 Weightlifting: snatch, clean and jerk; Olympic; Karnam Malleswari (bronze 2000, the first Indian woman to win an Olympic medal) and Mirabai Chanu (silver, Tokyo 2020).
  • SPT-11.5 Powerlifting, strongman, bodybuilding, CrossFit, arm wrestling: strength competitions outside the Olympics.
  • SPT-11.6 Yoga as sport (yogasana): competitive yogasana is in Khelo India and the National Games; International Yoga Day (21 June, since 2015).
  • SPT-11.7 Dance sport: ballroom and breaking (breakdance, Olympic only at Paris 2024).

sections.title: Combat sports and martial arts
sections.html:
Before you start — SPT-12. Combat sports have the oldest roots of all (wrestling is in the earliest art). Many Asian martial arts are also philosophies of self-discipline.
  • SPT-12.1 Wrestling: freestyle and Greco-Roman; United World Wrestling; Indian kushti in the akhara (mud pit), Great Gama (undefeated in the early 20th century); Khashaba Dadasaheb Jadhav won independent India's first individual Olympic medal (bronze, Helsinki 1952); Sushil Kumar (2008, 2012), Sakshi Malik (2016), Bajrang Punia, Ravi Dahiya, Aman Sehrawat (bronze, 2024).
  • SPT-12.2 Boxing: modern rules from the Marquess of Queensberry (1867); amateur and professional; Muhammad Ali; India's M. C. Mary Kom (six-time world champion, Olympic bronze 2012), Vijender Singh (2008), Lovlina Borgohain (2020), Nikhat Zareen.
  • SPT-12.3 Judo: founded by Kanō Jigorō at the Kodokan, Tokyo (1882); Olympic since 1964.
  • SPT-12.4 Karate (Okinawa), taekwondo (Korea; Olympic since 2000), kung fu / wushu (China; Asian Games), aikido, kendo, sumo (Japan's national sport), jiu-jitsu (Brazilian jiu-jitsu).
  • SPT-12.5 Fencing: foil, épée, sabre; from duelling schools; Olympic since 1896; Bhavani Devi was India's first Olympic fencer (2021).
  • SPT-12.6 Kickboxing, Muay Thai, savate, sambo, MMA (mixed martial arts; the UFC since 1993).
  • SPT-12.7 Indian martial arts: kalaripayattu (Kerala; with weapons and healing), silambam (Tamil Nadu, staff), thang-ta (Manipur, sword and spear), gatka (Punjab, Sikh), mardani khel (Maharashtra), lathi khela (Bengal), pari-khanda (Bihar); several are in the Khelo India Games.

sections.title: Cue sports, bowling, darts and indoor athletics
sections.html:
Before you start — SPT-13. Precision games of the club, the pub and the hall. Snooker was invented in India.
  • SPT-13.1 Billiards: English billiards, carom (French), pool (American, eight-ball and nine-ball); India's Pankaj Advani has won more than 25 world titles in billiards and snooker; Wilson Jones (world amateur billiards champion, 1958) and Geet Sethi.
  • SPT-13.2 Snooker: devised by British army officers at Jabalpur in 1875 (credited to the young officer Neville Chamberlain, later Colonel Sir Neville Chamberlain, not the prime minister) and codified at Ootacamund (Ooty) in 1882; the World Championship at the Crucible, Sheffield (since 1977).
  • SPT-13.3 Ten-pin bowling, nine-pin, duckpin, candlepin; World Bowling.
  • SPT-13.4 Darts: England; the PDC and WDF world championships; huge TV following.
  • SPT-13.5 Indoor athletics, indoor rowing, indoor cycling, climbing walls, table football (foosball), air hockey.

parts.title: Mind Games
parts.intro: About this Part. Games won by thinking: board games, cards, tiles, puzzles, words and quizzes. Some are pure skill (chess, Go), some mix skill and luck (backgammon, bridge, poker), and some are pure luck (Snakes and Ladders).

sections.title: Board games
sections.html:
Before you start — SPT-14. Board games are among the oldest human inventions (SPT-00.01). India gave the world chess, pachisi (Ludo) and Snakes and Ladders.

  • Chess: from Indian chaturanga (SPT-00.03); FIDE (founded Paris, 1924); the first official world champion was Wilhelm Steinitz (1886). Viswanathan Anand became India's first grandmaster (1988) and world champion (2000; undisputed 2007–2013). D. Gukesh became the youngest undisputed world champion (Singapore, December 2024, aged 18). In April 2026 Javokhir Sindarov (Uzbekistan) won the Candidates Tournament to challenge Gukesh, and R. Vaishali won the Women's Candidates. India won both gold medals at the 2024 Chess Olympiad (Budapest); Divya Deshmukh won the 2025 Women's World Cup.
  • Xiangqi (Chinese chess, with a river and cannons), shogi (Japanese chess, where captured pieces return), makruk (Thai chess), janggi (Korean chess).
  • Chess variants: Chess960 (Fischer Random), blitz and bullet, correspondence chess, chess problems and studies.

  • Go (weiqi, baduk): China, more than 2,500 years old; black and white stones on a 19×19 grid; AlphaGo (DeepMind) beat Lee Sedol in 2016, a landmark for AI.
  • Draughts (checkers), Reversi/Othello, Nine Men's Morris, Hex, Connect Four.
  • Aadu puli attam (goats and tigers): a South Indian hunt game; similar "hunt games" are played across Asia (the Nepali bagh-chal).
  • Mancala family: pallanguzhi (Tamil Nadu), oware (West Africa), bao (East Africa).

  • Senet and the Royal Game of Ur (see SPT-00.01).
  • Backgammon: from the Persian nard; skill and dice.
  • Pachisi and chaupar: the cross-shaped Indian race game played with cowrie shells; Akbar's giant courtyard board at Fatehpur Sikri. It became Ludo (patented in England, 1896) and the American Parcheesi.
  • Snakes and Ladders: from the Indian Moksha Patam / Gyan Chaupar, a moral game where virtues are ladders and vices are snakes; taken to England in the 1890s.
  • Correction from the brief: Chinese checkers is not Chinese. It was invented in Germany (1892) as Stern-Halma and given the name "Chinese checkers" by American marketers in 1928.

  • Monopoly: from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game (1904), a critique of landlords; sold by Parker Brothers from 1935. India's Business (Trade) game is a local version.
  • Scrabble (Alfred Butts, 1938), Cluedo/Clue (1949), Risk (1957), Catan (Klaus Teuber, 1995), Ticket to Ride, Carcassonne, Pandemic: the "Eurogame" boom.
  • Carrom: South Asian finger-flick game; the International Carrom Federation (1988); India and Sri Lanka lead; often played at home and in clubs.
  • Tabletop and role-playing games: Dungeons & Dragons (1974), miniature war games.

sections.title: Cards, tiles, puzzles, words and quizzes
sections.html:
• SPT-15.1 Playing cards: invented in Tang-dynasty China; spread through the Islamic world (Mamluk cards) to Europe in the 1370s; the French suits (hearts, diamonds, clubs, spades). India's ganjifa, round painted cards of the Mughal court and the Dashavatara sets of Odisha and Sawantwadi.
  • SPT-15.2 Card games: bridge (the World Bridge Federation, 1958; a medal sport at the 2018 Asian Games, where India won gold in men's pairs), rummy, teen patti, poker (skill and chance; real-money versions are now banned online in India), solitaire, uno; trading-card games such as Magic: The Gathering and Pokémon.
  • SPT-15.3 Tile games: mahjong (China, 19th century), dominoes, rummikub.
  • SPT-15.4 Puzzles: the jigsaw (John Spilsbury, London, 1760s, as a geography lesson); the crossword (Arthur Wynne, New York World, 1913); sudoku (Howard Garns's "Number Place", 1979; named by Nikoli, Japan, 1984); the Rubik's Cube (Ernő Rubik, 1974) and speedcubing; tangram (China).
  • SPT-15.5 Word games: Scrabble, Boggle, Wordle (2021), antakshari (the Indian song-chain game), shabd-khoj (word search), riddles (paheli).
  • SPT-15.6 Quizzes: Bournvita Quiz Contest (Derek O'Brien), Mastermind India, Kaun Banega Crorepati (2000, from Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?), university quiz clubs, the Tata Crucible; quiz master Siddhartha Basu.
  • SPT-15.7 Memory and mental sports: mental calculation, memory championships, the Mind Sports Olympiad.

parts.title: Digital Games and Esports
parts.intro: About this Part. Video games are the largest entertainment industry in the world by revenue. This Part maps their kinds, platforms and competitive scene. See also: TEC (computing), MOV (games and film).

sections.title: Video games and esports
sections.html:
• Action and platform (Super Mario Bros., 1985), adventure, role-playing (RPG) (The Legend of Zelda, Final Fantasy), shooter (first-person: Doom, Counter-Strike; battle royale: PUBG, Fortnite, Free Fire), strategy (real-time: StarCraft; turn-based: Civilization), MOBA (League of Legends, Dota 2), sports and racing (FIFA/EA Sports FC, Gran Turismo), fighting (Street Fighter), puzzle (Tetris, 1984), simulation and sandbox (The Sims, Minecraft), rhythm, horror, casual and mobile (Candy Crush, Ludo King).

  • Early: Tennis for Two (1958), Spacewar! (1962), Pong (Atari, 1972).
  • Arcade (1970s–80s: Space Invaders, Pac-Man); home consoles (Atari 2600, Nintendo Famicom/NES 1983, Sega, Sony PlayStation 1994, Xbox 2001, Nintendo Switch 2017); PC; handhelds (Game Boy 1989); mobile (Snake on Nokia phones, 1997; smartphones from 2007); VR and AR (Pokémon Go, 2016); cloud gaming.
  • Indian games and studios: Ludo King (Gametion, 2016), Raji: An Ancient Epic, Indian mobile studios; BGMI (India's version of PUBG Mobile).

  • Titles and tournaments: League of Legends World Championship, Dota 2's The International, Counter-Strike Majors, Valorant Champions, the FIFAe/EA FC competitions, BGMI and Free Fire leagues in India.
  • Multi-sport events: demonstration at the 2018 Asian Games; medal events at Hangzhou 2022; the IOC's Olympic Esports plans (check olympics.com for status).
  • Careers: players, coaches, analysts, casters, streamers, game designers; most earn modestly; a few earn millions.
  • India's law: the Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025 bans real-money online games and sets up support for esports and social games.

  • WHO lists gaming disorder in ICD-11 (2019) for severe cases; most players are not affected. Healthy habits: time limits, breaks, sleep first, play with people you know, no gambling-like spending (SPT-29).

parts.title: Traditional and Folk Games
parts.intro: About this Part. The games of villages, streets and festivals, many of them centuries old. Some became world sports (kabaddi, polo, badminton); many are fading and need recording. See also: CRO/KNT (traditional crafts), the Curriculum Index (Art and Culture).

sections.title: Traditional games of India
sections.html:
Before you start — SPT-17. India's traditional games need almost no equipment: a stick, a few stones, a line on the ground. The government's Khelo India programme (2018) and the Fit India Movement (2019) have brought several into schools. Names change from region to region; the common name comes first.

  • Kabaddi: two teams of seven; a raider crosses the line, tags opponents and must return in one breath while chanting "kabaddi"; ancient roots in Tamil Nadu and Punjab (forms: Sanjeevani, Gaminee, Amar, Punjabi circle style); Asian Games since 1990 (Iran won the men's gold in 2018; India regained it in 2022); Pro Kabaddi League (2014).
  • Kho-kho: a chase game of nine where chasers sit in a line facing opposite ways and "kho" (tag) a teammate to run; rules first written at Pune's Deccan Gymkhana (1914); India won both the men's and women's titles at the first Kho Kho World Cup (New Delhi, January 2025); Ultimate Kho Kho league (2022).
  • Atya-patya (Maharashtra), langdi (hopping tag), chor-police, chhupan-chhupai (hide and seek), oonch-neech ("high and low").

  • Gilli-danda: a small wooden peg (gilli) struck with a stick (danda), a cousin of cricket and the "tip-cat" of Europe; called kitti-pullu in Tamil Nadu and chinni-dandu in Andhra Pradesh.
  • Pitthu / lagori / sat-tolia (seven stones): one team knocks down a stack of stones with a ball and rebuilds it while the other team tries to hit them.
  • Kanche (marbles, goti), lattoo (spinning top), gutte / pallanguzhi (five stones and seed-pit games), stapu (hopscotch, kith-kith), kite flying (patangbazi; Uttarayan in Gujarat, 14 January).

  • Kushti / pehlwani in the akhara (SPT-12.1); mallakhamb (SPT-11.3); kalaripayattu, silambam, thang-ta, gatka (SPT-12.7); inbuan (Mizo wrestling); mukna (Manipuri wrestling); tug of war (rassa-kashi; Olympic 1900–1920).

  • Vallam kali (Kerala snake-boat races, SPT-06.7); kambala (Karnataka buffalo race in paddy fields); jallikattu (Tamil Nadu bull-taming, upheld by the Supreme Court in 2023 under the state's amended law); bullock-cart races (Maharashtra, Punjab); camel races (Pushkar and Bikaner fairs).
  • Ethics note: animal sports raise welfare questions; courts and laws have changed several times; the website presents both the cultural case and the welfare case.

  • Manipur: sagol kangjei (polo), yubi lakpi (coconut rugby), khong kangjei (hockey on foot).
  • Punjab: the Kila Raipur Rural Olympics (near Ludhiana, since 1933), with bullock-cart races and strength events; kabaddi circle style.
  • Himachal Pradesh: thoda (a folk archery battle from the Mahabharata).
  • Rajasthan and Gujarat: kabaddi, kite flying, chaupar (SPT-14.3).
  • North-east: Naga wrestling, Mizo inbuan, Assam's dhopkhel (a ball game of the Bihu season).
  • Indian board games: chaturanga, pachisi/chaupar, Moksha Patam, aadu puli attam, pallanguzhi (Part 4).

sections.title: Traditional games of the world
sections.html:
Before you start — SPT-18. Every country has its folk games; UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage lists include several. See also: INS (instruments of the same festivals).
  • SPT-18.1 Ball and stick games: the Mesoamerican ballgame (ulama survives in Mexico); cuju (China); kemari (Japan); calcio storico (Florence, a rough 16th-century football); hurling and Gaelic football (Ireland); pelota (Basque), chinlone (Myanmar, cane ball).
  • SPT-18.2 Wrestling traditions: sumo (Japan), Kırkpınar oil wrestling (Turkey, by tradition since 1346), schwingen (Switzerland), glíma (Iceland), ssireum (Korea), Senegalese laamb, Mongolian bökh.
  • SPT-18.3 Festivals of games: Naadam (Mongolia: wrestling, horse racing and archery), the Highland Games (Scotland: caber toss, hammer), the Nomad Games (Central Asia), Kila Raipur (India).
  • SPT-18.4 Horse and animal games: buzkashi (Afghanistan, Central Asia), chovgan (Azerbaijani polo), camel racing (Gulf), pato (Argentina's national game).
  • SPT-18.5 Throwing and target games: pétanque and boules (France), bocce (Italy), kubb (Sweden), jianzi (Chinese shuttlecock kicking), sepak takraw (South-East Asia).
  • SPT-18.6 Children's games everywhere: hopscotch, marbles, tops, cat's cradle, skipping rope, tag, hide-and-seek: the same games turn up in every continent, a sign of shared human play.

sections.title: Parasports and inclusive games
sections.html:
Before you start — SPT-19. Parasports began in rehabilitation hospitals after the Second World War. Today the Paralympics are the second-largest multi-sport event. Classification groups athletes by how their impairment affects their sport, so competition is fair.
  • SPT-19.1 Origins: Ludwig Guttmann's Stoke Mandeville Games for wounded veterans (England, 1948); the first Paralympic Games (Rome, 1960); the International Paralympic Committee (1989).
  • SPT-19.2 Paralympic sports: para athletics, para swimming, wheelchair basketball, wheelchair rugby, wheelchair tennis, para badminton, para archery, para shooting, sitting volleyball, boccia, goalball (for blind athletes, with a ball that has bells), blind football, para powerlifting, para canoe, para cycling, wheelchair fencing.
  • SPT-19.3 Other movements: the Deaflympics (Paris, 1924), the Special Olympics (for people with intellectual disabilities; founded by Eunice Kennedy Shriver, 1968), the Invictus Games (for wounded service members, 2014), the World Dwarf Games.
  • SPT-19.4 Blind cricket and other adapted games: blind cricket (a ball with ball-bearings that rattle; World Cups since 1998; India won the T20 World Cups of 2012, 2017 and 2022), wheelchair cricket, deaf cricket, adaptive chess (tactile boards).
  • SPT-19.5 India's Paralympians: Murlikant Petkar (India's first Paralympic gold, swimming, 1972), Devendra Jhajharia (javelin gold 2004 and 2016), Avani Lekhara (shooting gold 2020 and 2024), Sumit Antil (javelin gold 2020 and 2024), Sheetal Devi (archer without arms, Paralympic bronze 2024), Pramod Bhagat, Mariyappan Thangavelu; India won 29 medals (7 gold) at Paris 2024, its best ever.
  • SPT-19.6 Inclusive play: unified sports (players with and without disabilities together), accessible playgrounds, adapted PE in schools, the language of respect ("athlete with a disability", not "victim").

sections.title: The big stories of sport
sections.html:
• SPT-21.1 Codification: why 19th-century Britain wrote rules for so many games (railways, public schools, clubs, newspapers, the Empire); India's part in badminton, snooker and polo.
  • SPT-21.2 The amateur ideal and its end: the Olympics banned professionals for decades (Jim Thorpe was stripped of his medals in 1913, restored in 1982); professionals were fully admitted from the 1980s–90s.
  • SPT-21.3 Sport and empire: cricket in India and the Caribbean; C. L. R. James and Ashis Nandy on cricket as both colonial and anti-colonial (SPT-28); Mohun Bagan's barefoot win over the East Yorkshire Regiment in the 1911 IFA Shield.
  • SPT-21.4 Broadcasting and money: radio (AIR cricket commentary from the 1930s–40s), TV (Doordarshan's 1982 Asian Games in colour), satellite TV and Kerry Packer's World Series Cricket (1977), streaming rights worth billions.
  • SPT-21.5 The rise of women's sport: from the first women at the 1900 Olympics to equal numbers of men and women at Paris 2024 (the first "gender-equal" Games by athlete quota); Billie Jean King's "Battle of the Sexes" (1973); equal prize money at the Grand Slams; women's leagues (WPL, WSL); the Indian women's cricket World Cup of 2025.
  • SPT-21.6 Boycotts and politics: the apartheid sports boycott of South Africa (1960s–1991), the Moscow 1980 and Los Angeles 1984 boycotts, the Munich massacre (1972), the Black Power salute (Mexico City, 1968).
  • SPT-21.7 Esports and the digital age: SPT-16.

sections.title: Sports science, medicine, doping and technology
sections.html:
Before you start — SPT-27. Modern sport is a laboratory: of the body, of fairness and of technology. See also: TEC (sensors, cameras, AI), COK (nutrition).
  • SPT-27.1 Exercise physiology: aerobic and anaerobic energy; VO₂ max; altitude training (Kenyan and Ethiopian runners, Iten and the Rift Valley); heat and hydration.
  • SPT-27.2 Biomechanics: the physics of the javelin throw, the fast-bowling action, the high-jump flop, the golf swing; motion-capture and force plates.
  • SPT-27.3 Sports nutrition: carbohydrates for endurance, protein for repair, iron and vitamin D; Indian vegetarian athletes; supplements can be contaminated, so athletes must check (SPT-27.6).
  • SPT-27.4 Sports medicine and injuries: ACL tears (more common in women footballers), concussion protocols (cricket's concussion substitute since 2019), overuse in young athletes, return-to-play rules; physiotherapists and sports doctors.
  • SPT-27.5 Sports psychology: goal setting, visualisation, pre-performance routines, pressure and "choking", flow (SPT-28.2), mental health (Naomi Osaka, Simone Biles, Ben Stokes spoke openly).
  • SPT-27.6 Doping and anti-doping: the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA, 1999) and the World Anti-Doping Code; India's NADA (2005); the Ben Johnson (1988) and Lance Armstrong (stripped of seven Tour titles, 2012) cases; state-sponsored doping in Russia (the McLaren Report, 2016); "strict liability": athletes are responsible for what is in their bodies.
  • SPT-27.7 Fairness debates: sex testing and eligibility rules; the Dutee Chand case at the Court of Arbitration for Sport (2015); transgender participation policies set by each federation; classification in parasport (SPT-19).
  • SPT-27.8 Officiating technology: Hawk-Eye ball-tracking (tennis from 2006, cricket DRS from 2008–09), goal-line technology (FIFA World Cup 2014), VAR (World Cup 2018), semi-automated offside (2022), UltraEdge and snickometer, TMO in rugby, photo finish and electronic timing.
  • SPT-27.9 Equipment technology: carbon-plated running shoes, the full-body swimsuits banned in 2010, aluminium bats (banned in cricket after Dennis Lillee, 1979), smart balls, wearables and GPS vests; data analytics ("Moneyball").

parts.title: Ideas: Play, Philosophy, Psychology and Society

sections.title: Why we play, and what sport does to us
sections.html:
Before you start — SPT-28. Philosophers, psychologists and historians have asked what play is, why competition grips us and what sport does to nations. See also: BOK-20 (ideas), MUS-22 (music and the mind).

  • Johan Huizinga, Homo Ludens (1938): play is older than culture and lies at its root; play happens in a "magic circle" with its own rules.
  • Roger Caillois, Man, Play and Games (1958): four kinds of play: agôn (competition), alea (chance), mimicry (role-play) and ilinx (vertigo, such as swings and roller-coasters).
  • Bernard Suits, The Grasshopper (1978): a game is "the voluntary attempt to overcome unnecessary obstacles" (SPT-00.05).
  • Indian ideas: lila (divine play, the world as Krishna's play); krida in Sanskrit texts; the Mahabharata's dice game as a lesson on chance and dharma.

  • Flow (Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, 1990): total absorption when challenge matches skill.
  • Motivation: intrinsic (joy) and extrinsic (medals, money); why young athletes quit when sport stops being fun.
  • Home advantage, the "hot hand" (once called a myth, now debated with new data), choking under pressure.

  • Fandom (SPT-00.06): belonging, identity and rivalry.
  • Nationalism: George Orwell called international sport "war minus the shooting" ("The Sporting Spirit", 1945); sport can also build peace (Ping-Pong Diplomacy, the 2018 joint Korean team).
  • Cricket and India: C. L. R. sections.title: Playing, watching and gaming well
sections.html:
Before you start — SPT-29. For readers of every age who want to start a sport, understand the rules, watch well, run a games night or game healthily. Dates and websites carry a "checked on" date on the site.
  • SPT-29.1 How much activity: the WHO recommends at least 150–300 minutes of moderate (or 75–150 of vigorous) activity a week for adults, plus muscle-strengthening twice a week; children and teenagers an average of 60 minutes a day.
  • SPT-29.2 Starting a sport at any age: start with what you enjoy; join a club or group; learn basic skills from a coach; build up slowly (the "10 per cent a week" rule for runners); older adults can start walking, swimming, yoga, table tennis, badminton, pickleball.
  • SPT-29.3 Rules in plain words: one-page explainers for cricket (lbw, DRS, the follow-on), football (offside), tennis (scoring "love", deuce), kabaddi (raid, bonus line), chess (castling, en passant).
  • SPT-29.4 Safety: warm up and cool down; helmets and guards; heat and hydration in Indian summers; concussion: "if in doubt, sit them out"; safeguarding of children in sport.
  • SPT-29.5 Where to watch and follow: official broadcasters and apps (dated), free-to-air rules for major events in India (Prasar Bharati), official federation sites, radio commentary; avoid pirated streams.
  • SPT-29.6 Board-game and quiz nights: pick games by group size and time; teach in five minutes; include older and younger players; Indian classics (carrom, Ludo, chaupar, antakshari).
  • SPT-29.7 Healthy gaming: time limits, breaks every hour, no screens before sleep, parental controls, beware loot boxes and real-money games (illegal online in India since 2025), play with friends you know.
  • SPT-29.8 Careers in sport: athlete, coach, physio, analyst, referee, sports journalist, sports management, esports; the Sports Authority of India (SAI) schemes and Khelo India scholarships.

sections.title: Editor's notes (corrections and decisions on the brief)
sections.html:
1. "Chinese checkers" is a German game (1892), renamed in the USA (SPT-14.3).
  2. Snakes and Ladders and Ludo are credited to their Indian originals (Moksha Patam and pachisi).
  3. Badminton and snooker are given their Indian birthplaces (Pune and Jabalpur), with the British officers who codified them.
  4. The William Webb Ellis story (rugby) and the 776 BCE Olympic start date are marked as tradition.
  5. Indoor and outdoor: sports played in both settings are listed once, in their usual home, with cross-links.
  6. Animal sports carry an ethics note rather than a verdict.
  7. "Every sport ever" cannot fit one booklet: the index gives the master hierarchy, a 30-sport register and a 14-event register, and the website grows a page per sport.
  8. Latest results were checked on 3 November 2026. The 2026 Women's Ballon d'Or and the 2026 Formula One champion were not confirmed at the time of checking, so they are not stated.
  9. Added beyond the brief: India's online-gaming law (2025), fairness debates, officiating technology, caste and access, careers in sport, the gender-equal Paris Games, and India's 2030 Commonwealth Games.
